# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

# Critical Reading of Varga & Holm's Comment

Sections 1–5 of this comment are strong and largely confirm the concerns about the Halden pilot. The core arithmetic is correct:

- 34.6 / 40.3 is a 14.1% fall in hours.
- 95.1 / 0.8 gives +18.9%, and 98.4 / 0.859 gives +14.6%.
- 95.4 / 86.1 gives +10.8%.
- 1.014 / 1.041 gives about −2.6% in real revenue.

The comment's main conclusion, however, does not follow from its own evidence. It also ignores the strongest evidence against that conclusion.

## What the comment does well

- **Attrition.** This is a genuine discovery. The working paper said the nine withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". In fact, 7 of the 9 left after the reduced schedule had started, and 6 cited workload or output problems. If this is accurate, the original paper misreported its sample.
- **Output measure.** In 23 organisations, the managers' ratings can be checked against records. The gap is systematic: managers rated output higher in 19 of the 23.
- **Hours.** Actual hours come from time-tracking logs, so the comment doesn't rely on schedules.
- **Corrections shown step by step.** Table 2 applies each correction separately, so readers can see how much each one matters.
- **Data note.** It is candid that the corrected estimates apply only to the subsets that could be corrected.

## 1. The conclusion overreaches, in steps

The claim gets stronger as the paper goes on:

- The abstract says the four problems "account for **most** of the reported gain".
- Section 6 says the residual is "**plausibly** a novelty effect".
- The conclusion says the gains are "**entirely** an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty".

The corrected estimate is still +10.8%. The novelty argument for the residual rests on one survey measure (point 5). So "most" is supported; "entirely" is not. The data note concedes that the corrected figures describe non-random subsets, yet the conclusion generalises to "reduced-hours schemes" as a whole.

## 2. It ignores the Varden case-processing result

The comment calls Varden's counter-office result "the most reliable finding in the literature". It never mentions Varden's other stratum. Varden's case-processing offices used every method this comment recommends: randomisation, record-based output, and actual hours from timesheets. They showed **+12.5% output per actual hour (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4)** at nine months, which is already later than the "month ten" when, by the comment's own extrapolation, energy would be back to baseline.

That result is the most direct test of the "entirely an artifact" claim, and it contradicts it. The Varden trial cannot rule out a novelty effect, since staff knew their assignment. But a comment that relies on Varden for one stratum cannot leave out the other.

## 3. Attrition is described but never corrected

The abstract says "correcting the first three" problems gives 10.8%, and attrition is the first of them. Table 2, however, corrects only output and hours. The 17-organisation subset contains survivors only. The comment never estimates how much attrition matters. A simple bounding exercise would do it: assign the withdrawers a plausible range of outputs and include them in the mean. The comment itself recommends analysing "all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw", but does not do so. Also, only 8 of the 9 exit reasons are accounted for (6 workload, 2 scheduling).

## 4. The hours breakdown doesn't add up

The comment says the gap between scheduled and actual hours comes from two sources:

- longer remaining days: +0.7 hours × 4 days = 2.8 hours
- work logged on the day off: 1.6 hours

Together these come to 4.4 hours above the 32 scheduled, which implies about 36.4 hours a week. The reported figure is 34.6. Either the components are measured on a different basis, perhaps a different subset or relative to a different day length, or one of them is wrong. This needs reconciling, because the hours correction drives most of the movement in Table 2.

## 5. The novelty argument is weak, and better data were available

- **Energy is not output.** A falling self-reported energy score does not show that output per hour fell.
- **The pilot collected monthly output indices.** The comment had the microdata. It could have tested directly whether output per hour declined from month 1 to month 6, at least in the organisations with records and time tracking. It did not.
- **The extrapolation is fragile.** It is a straight line through two points, and it doesn't quite match the comment's own figure. A decline from 0.61 to 0.29 over three months, continued linearly, reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten". Energy could just as easily level off.
- **The burden-of-proof argument cuts both ways.** It is a fair reason not to claim a durable effect. It is not evidence that the effect is entirely novelty.

## 6. The meetings section misrepresents Varden

- The Varden authors did not present meetings "as a mechanism". They labelled the analysis unregistered and exploratory, noted that it rests on seven offices, said that a correlation "cannot establish a mechanism", and registered a confirmatory test. The comment criticises a claim Varden did not make.
- "Selected for analysis after the results were known" is not what Varden describes. The calendar data were collected in month six at managers' request. The analysis was unregistered, but the data were not gathered after the results were in.
- The comment discusses only the r = 0.71 correlation. The 3.8 v 7.1 hours-per-week difference in meeting time is a treated-versus-control comparison across all 14 randomised case-processing offices. That is stronger evidence that meeting time actually fell.
- The meetings hypothesis is also the main alternative to novelty. Cancelling meetings that persisted out of habit is a plausibly durable change. Dismissing it is what makes "entirely novelty" look like the only remaining explanation.

## 7. The record-based measure has validity problems of its own

The comment treats records as ground truth, but one listed record type is **"billable hours delivered"**. That is largely a measure of time worked. Using it as output partly re-imports the hours cut into the output index and pushes the record-based figure down. Tickets closed or units produced also miss quality and value. The comment should report the gap between manager ratings and records for each record type.

## 8. Small samples and no uncertainty

- None of the corrected estimates has a confidence interval. This includes the 10.8% that the conclusion rests on.
- The retail figure (−11.2%) comes from **three organisations**. Its close match with Varden's −11.4% is a coincidence of two very different settings, not a replication.
- The organisations with time-tracking software are probably concentrated in professional services and software, where billable-hours tracking is common. The corrected subset may therefore lean towards the sectors that performed best.

## 9. Smaller points

- **Deflator.** Consumer prices are a rough deflator for business revenue. Producer or sector-specific prices would be better. The direction of the conclusion, that real revenue fell, is probably right.
- **No control group.** The corrected 10.8% is still an uncontrolled before-and-after comparison. Economic conditions could bias it in either direction. The comment doesn't mention this, even though it applies to the estimate the comment treats as the residual.
- **The "negative finding".** "Where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output" is well supported. But in Varden it comes from a design that kept staffing fixed during unchanged opening hours. It shows what happens without extra hiring, not that reduced hours cannot work in coverage-bound roles.

## Overall assessment

The forensic work in Sections 1–5 is valuable:

- It exposes a misreported attrition story.
- It quantifies how much manager ratings overstate output.
- It roughly halves the Halden per-hour estimate using better hours data.

The interpretive sections are less careful. The step from "most of the gain is artifact" to "entirely artifact" depends on:

- a two-point extrapolation of a survey measure,
- a straw-man treatment of the Varden meetings analysis,
- omitting the one randomised result, Varden's case-processing stratum, that directly tests the claim.

A defensible conclusion would be that the Halden pilot overstated per-hour gains by more than half. The best controlled evidence suggests a real but modest gain in work not tied to presence, of uncertain durability, and a clear loss of output in coverage-bound work when staffing is held fixed.
